title: Design a Parking Lot
summary: The most-asked LLD question there is, and the one most often failed for the same reason: candidates model the world instead of the requirements. Here is the class design, the two decisions that actually get graded, and where the concurrency bug hides.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: This question has no algorithm in it. It is **entirely** a test of whether you can turn a vague brief into a class diagram without either over-modelling or hard-coding. The two decisions being graded are *how a spot is chosen* and *how the fee is computed* — and both are graded on whether you made them replaceable.
Design a parking lot. A vehicle arrives, is assigned a spot that fits it, and gets a ticket. On exit the system computes a fee from the time parked and frees the spot.

blocks.title: The failure mode is modelling the world
blocks.text: There is no credit for `Wheel`, `Colour`, or an `Owner` class. Every class you add has to be justified by a requirement someone stated. Interviewers cut candidates for a sprawling diagram far more often than for a small one.

items.title: Multiple floors, or one?
items.text: Changes whether `ParkingLot` holds spots or holds floors. Ask; do not assume a multi-storey car park because the phrase sounds impressive.

items.title: How many vehicle types, and can a big spot take a small car?
items.text: This single answer decides the allocation strategy. If a motorcycle may take a car spot, allocation becomes a fit problem rather than a lookup.

items.title: How is the fee calculated?
items.text: Flat rate, hourly, first hour free, different per vehicle type, weekend rates? You will not implement all of them — you will implement one behind an interface.

items.title: Multiple entry and exit gates?
items.text: This is the concurrency question in disguise. Two gates assigning the same spot is the bug they are looking for.

items.title: Reservations, or first come first served?
items.text: Reservations add a whole state to the spot lifecycle. Confirm it is out of scope before you skip it.

blocks.caption: Agreed before any class is drawn.
rows: Park a vehicle: assign a fitting free spot, issue a ticket
Unpark: compute the fee from duration, free the spot
Report free spots per floor and per type
Assignment is O(1), not a scan of every spot
Two gates must never be handed the same spot

blocks.title: The shape that gets full marks
blocks.caption: `ParkingLot` coordinates and owns nothing clever. The two things that vary — **which spot** and **how much** — are interfaces, and that is the entire point of the exercise.

blocks.title: Two interfaces, and say why
blocks.text: *“Allocation and pricing are the two things every parking lot operator wants different, so they are the two things I am putting behind interfaces.”* That sentence is worth more than the rest of the diagram. It shows you know **strategy** is a response to a requirement, not a pattern you sprinkle on.
Allocation — the decision they are grading
The naive implementation scans every spot on every floor. It is O(n) per car and it is what most candidates write.

blocks.title: Say what “fits” means
blocks.text: `SpotSize.fittingFrom(MOTORCYCLE)` returning `[SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE]` encodes *a motorcycle may use a bigger spot but never a smaller one*. Making that ordering explicit — rather than an `if` ladder — is the difference between a design and a script.

blocks.title: Round up, and use a monotonic clock
blocks.text: Two real bugs live here. Rounding **down** means a 59-minute stay is free — pricing bugs are the ones that reach production. And computing duration from wall-clock time means a daylight-saving shift or an NTP correction can produce a negative stay. Store an instant, not a local time.
Two entry gates, one free spot. Both threads read `free.size() > 0`, both pop, one gets a null or the same spot twice. This is the single most common defect in submitted answers.

items: **Do not** lock the whole lot — that serialises every gate in the building.
Per-level, per-size pools mean two gates contend only when they want the same size on the same floor.
`freeCount` becomes an estimate the moment there are concurrent writers. That is fine for a display board; say so rather than pretending it is exact.

items.title: Show free spots on a display board per floor
items.text: O(1) if each level keeps a counter per size. The moment you need this, the O(n) scan design is dead — which is a good argument for the deque design up front.

items.title: Add electric-vehicle spots with charging
items.text: A new `SpotSize`? No — a new *capability*. `Spot` gets a set of features, and allocation filters on them. This is the question that separates enum-thinking from attribute-thinking.

items.title: Handle a lost ticket
items.text: Charge the maximum daily rate. The interesting part is that this is a *policy*, so it belongs in `FeeStrategy`, not in an `if` inside `unpark`.

items.title: Support reservations
items.text: The spot lifecycle grows a `RESERVED` state with an expiry, and allocation must skip reserved spots without leaking them if the holder never arrives.

items.title: Multiple lots in a city
items.text: The pivot to HLD: a lot becomes a service, the display board becomes a read replica, and consistency between “spot free” and “spot taken” becomes eventual.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: Lot full → `park` returns empty, and the caller decides what that means. Do not throw for an expected outcome.
Unpark with a ticket that is already settled → reject, do not double-charge and do not double-free the spot.
A vehicle type with no spot size that fits at all → rejected at the gate, not after issuing a ticket.
Exit time earlier than entry time → clamp to zero and log; never return a negative fee.
A spot released twice must not appear twice in the free pool.

rows: Only classes a stated requirement needs
O(1) pools per level and size
Strategy interfaces for allocation and pricing
An explicit ordering of fitting sizes
Names the two-gate race and makes the claim atomic

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–6** clarify: floors, types, fit rules, gates, pricing. **6–12** write the requirements list on the board and get agreement. **12–20** classes and the two interfaces. **20–32** code `park`, `unpark`, and one allocator. **32–38** the two-gate race. **38–45** one follow-up, ideally EV spots — it is the one that shows attribute-thinking.
